extracted.intended_audience: research and academic mathematicians and technical users evaluating/choosing computer algebra systems (CAS)
extracted.subtask_description: Comparative review checklist and evaluation criteria for symbolic/numeric computer algebra systems (Derive, Maple, Mathematica, Reduce) covering correctness, performance, interfaces, language features, graphics, and I/O/export. Intended to guide selection and benchmarking of CAS for various mathematical tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intended focus / suitability for project size
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the product is aimed at quick small calculations or medium/large projects (e.g., 'MathCAD's focus on quick and dirty calculations rather than medium/large projects').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the reviewer's note on product focus to judge fit for long projects; the reviewer warns that true test is a long project which cannot be reasonably simulated in short review sessions and recommends checking books/examples for larger projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: User interface quality and ergonomics
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the quality and polish of the user interface (e.g., 'Maple's DOS interface ... is by far the slickest DOS interface', 'Mathematica for Windows' notebook interface ... lets you produce live documents', 'Reduce ... a terrible interface').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider menu systems, full-screen editor support, customizable menus, notebook features, and how easy it is to edit/recall previous commands; interface impacts productivity and learning curve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardware/resource requirements and low-end performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Check minimum/ recommended hardware and RAM and how the product performs on older/limited machines (e.g., 'All programs but Derive require a 386 or better. All but Derive recommend a coprocessor. Derive doesn't need (or use) more than 640K of RAM. The others recommend at least 2M of RAM, and Mathematica will perform poorly without 6 or 8MB').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use resource usage to judge suitability for older hardware, notebooks, or low-memory environments; Derive's low-resource usage is an advantage for XTs, while Mathematica needs more RAM for good performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing / performance on benchmark problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure runtime on representative short and medium-length problems under controlled hardware (the review used a 386/25 with 15 MB RAM; timing differences were reported in Figure 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing tests were done on short problems; reviewer notes that differences are much less significant than in 1990 and not regarded as very important now. Include note when problems were done by hand (BH) or could not be done (NA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness and correctness of algebraic simplification
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether simplification routines produce expected algebraic simplifications (examples: 'neither Mathematica nor Maple would simplify Sqrt(4+2 Sqrt(3))' and 'both got the wrong answer on the gravitational potential problem (3c)').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test a variety of simplification cases (algebraic number recognition, factorization over algebraic domains, trigonometric & nested radicals). Note any workarounds (e.g., Mathematica's Recognize, Maple's routines, Reduce factorization over algebraic domain).

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and numerical control
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess support for arbitrary precision and control of rounding/precision (examples: using 50 place accuracy for Hilbert matrix inversion; Derive remark that 42 places suffice because of rational approximation methods; use of 'precision', 'SetPrecision', 'on rounded/off rounded').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check ability to set precision, do high-precision numeric tasks, and estimate required decimal places for desired accuracy (the review requested estimating decimal places to achieve identity to one part in 10^(-6)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory management and ability to handle large/long computations
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine how the CAS behaves on large problems (example: Hilbert 30x30 inverse caused out-of-memory in Derive when examining the answer; reviewer notes long projects cannot be reasonably simulated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test creating/inspecting large matrices, multi-step computations; note when systems require separate sessions or produce out-of-memory errors and whether they allow continuing work after large computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language expressiveness and programming constructs
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the power of the system's programming language: pattern matching, IF, iterative constructions, functions/procedures, noncommutative rules, and ability to write moderately complex algorithms (examples: Derive's IF enabled iterative constructions; Reduce demonstrated complex procedures; Mathematica's pattern/rule definitions for Clifford algebra; Maple scripts and packages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider availability of control structures (IF, loops, ITERATE), ability to define custom rules/patterns, packaging mechanism (Needs/with/loadlib), and ease of implementing domain-specific algorithms (e.g., Clifford algebra, Feigenbaum programs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Built-in symbolic capabilities (integration, differentiation, limits, sums, factoring)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess built-in symbolic operations: differentiation, symbolic integration (including definite integrals), limits, symbolic sums, polynomial factoring, multivariate factoring, and special functions (the review enumerates many problems under these headings and notes which systems succeeded/failed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test a representative suite: tricky derivatives/integrals (3a-c), limits to infinity (4a,b), symbolic sums and factoring (5,10), and whether the system returns closed forms or fails/returns incorrect results (e.g., Maple returned a correct automated solution for a limit that others mishandled). Note when packages or manual intervention are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definite integrals and support for rigorous definite-integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether the CAS can handle definite integrals and infinite integrals symbolically; review notes that Reduce 'doesn't do definite integrals' and required hand solutions, while Maple/Mathematica provided symbolic or numeric results (examples in Problem 8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test definite integrals over infinite intervals and evaluate if answers are expressed in terms of known constants (pi, Gamma) or require manual steps; note where numeric alternatives (NIntegrate, Laplace transforms) are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for special algebraic domains (algebraic numbers, Gaussian integers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the system can factor or compute in algebraic number fields and nonstandard integer rings (example: Maple lacked Gaussian integer factoring at the time; Mathematica had built-in support with a flag 'GaussianIntegers -> True').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test factoring over algebraic number fields, ability to specify domains, and availability of built-in packages to handle these cases or whether manual Diophantine solving is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integer factorization and prime testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate integer factoring routines and prime-finding functions (examples: Derive, Maple, Mathematica, Reduce solutions for factoring and NextPrime; reviewer notes probabilistic approaches for NextPrime with guarantee in practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test large integer factoring, factoring over Gaussian integers, and next-prime computations; note algorithms used (probabilistic vs deterministic) and package dependencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule-based / noncommutative algebra support
rubrics_metrics.description: Check the ability to define and compute with custom algebraic rules and noncommutative operators (examples: Clifford algebra in 10 variables, custom noncommutative multiplication rules in Mathematica, Reduce, Maple).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test ability to express rules, enforce noncommutativity, and compute powers/expansions under those rules; evaluate whether implementation is awkward or straightforward and whether it requires many lines of code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numeric solvers for nonlinear systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess capabilities for numerical root-finding in systems of nonlinear equations, complex solutions, and root refinement (example: Mathematica's FindRoot and strategies for random starts found many roots; Reduce required a numeric package).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test FindRoot/num_solve functionality, starting-point strategies, complex arithmetic, duplicate removal and whether built-in methods exist or user code is required. Note run times and number of solutions found.

rubrics_metrics.name: ODE and recurrence-solving facilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate symbolic ODE solvers, Bernoulli/linear ODE handling, and recursion solvers (examples: DSolve, dsolve, odesolve, and custom recursion solvers provided in Maple/Reduce/Derive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test common ODEs, nonstandard forms, and linear recurrences; note where numeric solvers (NDSolve) are used instead of symbolic ones and where manual transformations (Bernoulli) are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphics capabilities and plotting quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess 2D/3D plotting, parametric plots, surface plots, polyhedra, contour plotting, and special graphics libraries (examples: 'Mathematica's graphics are special', 'Mathematica strong suit', 'Reduce has no graphics', 'Derive/Maple have varying support').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test parametric curves, 3D surfaces, polyhedra drawing (icosahedron), contour surfaces, and whether the system provides color, shading, and good primitives; note the availability of example galleries and vendor-supplied demos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphics export, printing, and file format support
rubrics_metrics.description: Check printing support and ability to save graphics as vector or bitmap files (examples: 'Derive has no explicit support for printing graphs or saving to a file', 'Maple can capture HPGL, Mathematica DOS can send EPS, Windows adds BMP and WMF', 'Maple has many printer supports').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify supported export formats (EPS, CGM, HPGL, PCX, TIFF, BMP, WMF), ability to print directly to laser printers, and workflows for saving graphics for desktop publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability and integration of external packages/libraries
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the ecosystem of external libraries and built-in packages (examples: Mathematica's Needs['...'] to load packages, Maple's with(linalg) or readlib, Reduce package load_package, some functionality available via internet or books).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check how easy it is to load and use add-on packages, whether common algorithms require third-party packages, and the documentation/availability of such packages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Export / code generation to external languages / formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate tools for translating mathematical expressions/programs to TeX and C (example: 'Derive can do C but not TeX; the other three can do both').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test automatic export to TeX, C, or other target languages and assess fidelity and convenience for embedding CAS output into publications or C programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maturity/stability and product roadmap
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider maturity of the product, frequency of upgrades, and vendor plans (examples: 'Reduce is not yet a mature product ... just starting to make the transition ... they are pushing to Windows', 'acsyma was not included ... vendor plans a new release later this year').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vendor release history, ongoing development (Windows ports, GUI improvements), and current stability reports to judge long-term viability and risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing, pricing, and student/academic discounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Document price points, availability of student editions and site/academic license discounts (the review lists prices and student editions for Derive, Maple, Mathematica, Reduce).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider total cost of ownership, availability of low-cost/student versions for teaching, and whether feature limitations apply to cheaper/student editions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copy protection and user-experience impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider copy-protection mechanisms and their effect on usability (example: 'Mathematica has added copy protection ... program records hardware information ... glitches that burn users ... unable to run QEMM with Mathematica without getting a four-question inquisition after EACH command').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh security vs user hassle; note historical pushback by users and potential interactions with system utilities. This can be a practical blocker in multi-user or constrained environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of worked examples and vendor-supplied demos
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether vendors supply extensive example solutions and demo projects to illustrate strengths (review included many vendor solutions for the 18 problem suite and extra graphics/examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check included example libraries and whether they cover advanced tasks (graphics, numerical experiments like Feigenbaum, Koch snowflake, rule-based algebra). These demonstrate practical capability and ease of learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior on edge-cases and discontinuities
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how the system treats discontinuities and avoids false algebraic simplifications (vendor note for Derive: 'most discontinuities such as tan(x) or sign(x) are not bridged, and false transformations such as arc tan(tan(x)) -> x are avoided').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test examples with branch-cut issues, sign/absolute values, and inverse-function simplifications; conservative behavior may avoid wrong simplifications but could return less-simplified results.
